extracted.intended_audience: brand managers, founders, in-house marketers, and design agency professionals evaluating or commissioning logo and identity work
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating logo and brand identity systems, with emphasis on strategic conviction, distinctiveness, rollout planning, and resistance to trend-driven 'blandification'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conviction-Based Identity / Corporate Spine
rubrics_metrics.description: A design failure was not aesthetic but a failure of corporate spine; brands must have the conviction to defend their identity choices rather than surrender to public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you decide to change your identity, do so with strategic depth that can withstand the initial 48-hour wave of public 'hate.' Defend the vision: explain the strategic shift and allow consumers time to adapt rather than reverting immediately. Treat identity as a core business asset, not a fashion accessory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness (Preserve High-Equity Assets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve distinctive brand assets (e.g., Gap's 'Blue Box' and high-equity serif); replacing them with generic elements erases the brand's visual beacon and distinctiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctiveness is a mechanical requirement for brand recall and mental availability. Avoid substituting unique visual anchors with high-frequency, undifferentiated elements. Work with experts who understand 'Distinctive Brand Assets' and build identity around recognisable cues rather than stripping them away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Blandification / Trend-Driven Modernisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernisation that strips personality (blandification) often results in invisibility — many 'modern' sans-serif marks converge into sameness, especially with AI tools producing generic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate 'modern' with 'the same as everyone else.' Resist AI- and trend-driven defaults (e.g., mass Helvetica-like marks). Prioritise radical visual difference and 'friction' to stand out in an AI-saturated market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typeface Frequency and Appropriateness (Helvetica Trap)
rubrics_metrics.description: High-frequency fonts like Helvetica can lead to brand invisibility because they are used so widely that the brain filters them out as 'background noise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Helvetica without a unique secondary visual asset risks low equity and recognisability. Choose typefaces that convey brand voice and, when using widely seen fonts, pair them with proprietary visual elements to retain distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Anchor / Enclosure (Distinctive Visual Anchor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brands need a 'visual anchor' — a shape, colour block, or enclosure (e.g., the Blue Box) that functions as a beacon in retail environments and peripheral vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems should include elements with sufficient visual weight and enclosure so consumers can scan and recognise the brand quickly. Tiny or hovering accents (small gradient squares) may lack the necessary anchoring effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friction as a Design Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction (unique ligatures, unusual colour pairings, 'clunky' serifs) makes the eye stop and wonder, building long-term memory and distinctiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce controlled friction deliberately rather than pursuing total minimalism. Friction is the opposite of blandification and is recommended as a hedge against AI-driven sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility Across Media (Gradient & Technical Consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain visual choices (like gradients) are difficult to reproduce consistently across different media and contexts, causing inconsistent brand expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fragile visual treatments that don't scale (tiny gradients, subtle effects). Test identity elements on lit signage, receipts, digital displays and print to ensure consistent reproduction; prefer forms that retain integrity in all use cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive/UX Principles (Scanability & Mental Availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must account for how the human brain scans retail environments — shapes and colours (not just reading) drive recognition; high-frequency elements reduce mental availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form and colour to create beacons; maintain contrast so logos register in peripheral vision. Validate designs with cognitive/UX research (e.g., recall testing) to ensure mental availability is preserved or improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process Discipline: Do Not Crowdsource Identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowdsourcing logo design or asking the public to 'help us decide' is a surrender of leadership and yields least-offensive, low-strategy outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Branding is strategic, not democratic. Avoid community vote-driven identity decisions; treat stakeholder engagement as research input, not a replacement for a curated strategic vision. Crowdsourcing signals lack of internal clarity and damages brand authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Design by Committee' / Maintain Consistent Design Vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Design by committee or overly iterative public input undermines strategic conviction and leads to diluted, risk-averse outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint clear decision-makers and ensure the brand team can defend and explain the rationale. Consistent vision correlates with better business outcomes (cited McKinsey finding: consistent design vision outperforms peers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rollout & Operational Planning (Physical + Digital Overhaul Costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new logo requires total physical and digital overhaul — signage, POS, packaging, internal documents — and operational costs can be substantial and immediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for production, disposal, emergency reorders and recovery periods. Model 'Total Cost of Retrieval' and consider environmental/legislative implications (circular economy levies). Avoid rushed unveils that trigger wasteful rework if reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis Preparedness & Backlash Handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect an initial wave of negative reaction to significant identity changes; prepare a communication plan and strategic response rather than immediate retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for PR and social media management, explain why changes were made, and allow consumers time to adapt. Surrendering quickly (e.g., within 6 days) signals weakness; have messaging that frames change as strategic and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Core Strategy as the Basis for Rebranding
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebrands must be grounded in a clear 'Brand Core Strategy' rather than aesthetics alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure identity decisions map to positioning, audience insights, and business goals. Work with teams/agencies that 'live the brand' and can translate strategy into distinct visual systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Selection & Internal Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on external agencies that don't 'live the brand' increases the risk of misaligned work and poor long-term outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select partners who understand the business, its heritage and long-term strategy. Ensure internal stakeholders retain ownership and can articulate and defend the strategic rationale for identity changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage Heritage When Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Reintroducing serifs, emblems or heritage cues (as Burberry did) can restore distinctiveness and reconnect with brand memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider heritage assets as valuable sources of distinctiveness; evaluate whether simplifying away heritage will harm recognisability. Use heritage thoughtfully to maintain or regain mental availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic Impact Assessment (Sales, Market Value, Waste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brand identity decisions can have immediate and measurable financial impacts — drops in sales, market depreciation, waste of printed materials, and associated remediation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate likely sales impact, market value changes, and inventory/asset costs. Include recovery periods and long-term brand equity effects in business case analyses for rebrands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding AI-Generated Sameness
rubrics_metrics.description: AI design tools accelerate 'clean, modern' defaults producing thousands of similar marks; relying on these outputs increases risk of anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AI tools cautiously; prioritise human-led strategic differentiation. If using generative tools, filter outputs through distinctiveness and heritage criteria rather than adopting 'perfectly balanced' defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Invisibility Diagnostic — Semantic Search
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic Search: can your brand be found by AI search agents (e.g., does your brand appear in top 3 citations for category queries)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate SEO/entity presence and optimise for category dominance. If invisible to AI search agents, the brand risks being overlooked by modern discovery channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Invisibility Diagnostic — Visual Trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual Trust: would a stranger mistake your website for a template or competitor if the logo was removed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess uniqueness of website visual DNA; if it reads like a template or competitor, invest in brand-specific visual systems to avoid being mistaken for generic players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Invisibility Diagnostic — Verbal Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal Impact: does your website copy rely on generic jargon (e.g., 'Synergy', 'Innovation') in primary paragraphs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differentiated, benefit-led messaging rather than cliché sector jargon to improve brand distinctiveness and perceived expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand Invisibility Diagnostic — Conversion Friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion Friction: how many fields must a lead fill out before contacting a human? (1–3 fields = frictionless; 8+ fields = high friction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce conversion friction to improve lead flow. Measure contact form complexity and time-to-human-response as part of brand experience evaluation.
